P1.evidence: Three-part frame — 'dive into what you're liking to achieve, what you're currently at, see if we can help you bridge that gap. If we can, I'll take you through how. If not, totally fine, I'll point you in the best direction.' Agreement taken ('All right. Perfect.'). Open question run. The rep also handled the environment well at the top, getting the prospect to put the phone on a stand.

P2.evidence: Age, height and weight taken. Nutrition covered adequately. Almost nothing else. Occupation was never asked at any point, which is why the ICP cannot be scored on 'successful'. Health conditions never asked. The pain was explored for duration and location but never for whether anyone has examined it. Training week was covered only as 'I go to the gym pretty frequently, do like weight training' with no follow-up on volume, split or days. Sleep and energy absent — from an athlete whose presenting complaint is recovery.

P3.evidence: Surface layer done properly — got the 200-205 lb target, the flexibility self-rating and the specific thing he cannot do ('I can't push myself as hard because I'm like feeling pain'). The bridge was attempted — 'is there also more of a mental goal that you have to that energy, confidence-wise?' — and the prospect closed it ('I have a good amount of energy, and I have a pretty good amount of confidence'). The rep accepted that and never reopened. No 'who else does this impact', nothing on family, identity or legacy. When asked what getting rid of the soreness would mean, the answer was 'It would feel great' and the rep did not push past it.

P4.evidence: Asked what he had tried and got a useful answer — Knees Over Toes and self-sourced lifting routines, both of which helped but not enough. Then stopped. Never asked why they did not fully work, never let him name the gap, never asked the root-cause question. This matters because the honest answer may be that nothing is structurally wrong with his approach and he simply likes trying things — 'me, I like to try different stuff, so I wanna see, like, what works best' — which is a weak buying position the rep never surfaced.

P5.evidence: One move ran and ran well: 'you would also, from what I'm hearing, think that if you don't change anything about it, it will keep getting worse?' → 'Uh, I would. say so, yeah.' That is a genuine consequence admission on a worsening four-year problem and it was the strongest lever on the call. The rep did not build on it — no settling question, no 'why not', no line in the sand — and by the time price landed twenty minutes later it had gone cold.

P6.evidence: The commitment check failed twice over. Asked whether the three pillars would get him there, he answered 'I hope so. I mean, I can only try and see if it works.' The rep challenged the word hope — correctly — and got 'I won't know until I try, but yeah.' That is not a yes. The 1-10 question was then asked twice and misunderstood both times, and the rep settled for 'I'm interested in trying to start as soon as possible' as the green light. The playbook says do not move forward without a clear YES; there was not one.

P11.evidence: Scored against the product actually sold. Payment was collected live and confirmed — 'I just put in my card information' and 'I saw indeed that the payment went through' — which is the only completed live collection in this batch. No onboarding call with Trevor and no agreement apply to Primal University. The rep did screen-share and walk him through the classroom, the foundations module and where to post an introduction, which is the nearest equivalent of step 4 and was done properly.

objection_plays.detail: Money was the objection and the play barely ran. No isolation question — the rep never asked whether anything besides finances was holding him back, so 'I hope so' and 'I can only try' were never resolved. No 'you're not in a should-I place, you're in a how place'. No financial picture at all: no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no credit cards, no assets. The rep went straight from 'What would be more affordable for you?' to a $200/month product. Given a stated $150 ceiling this may have been the right commercial call, but it is not the play.

Doubt surfaced clearly — 'I hope so. I mean, I can only try and see if it works' and 'I won't know until I try'. The rep ran one genuine OE-adjacent move, challenging the word hope: 'When it comes to hoping, do you feel like hope is the right strategy?' That is good instinct. But he then conceded the point himself ('Of course, you can only know so much beforehand, right? I also understand that. That's totally normal') and moved on, leaving the doubt live going into the price.

The prospect asked directly for a middle option — 'Do you have different packages? Is there a more affordable package? Because I'm still interested.' — and the rep declined to enumerate what exists, saying it would take forty minutes. There is no defined ladder between $6,000 one-to-one and $200/month group, and no scripted way to answer a prospect who wants one. Worth reading against the same rep improvising a $4,000 three-month tier three days earlier for a prospect who queried the price without asking for a cheaper option.

notes: Baseline was the weakest in the batch — occupation, health history, sleep, energy and training volume all skipped on an athlete presenting with a four-year recovery problem. The one strong moment was getting him to admit the pain will worsen if nothing changes, and it was never converted. He then moved to price with 'I hope so' as the commitment answer. The sale that resulted was a $199/month product against a $6,000 offer, closed on the prospect's budget rather than on any value the call built.
